# Ref_Auction Playbook

**On budget tracking:**
When I see my budget displayed alongside my bid, I will verify it immediately. I notice I recorded inconsistent budgets (jumping from 20 to 82, then to 991) which suggests I either misread or mismanaged my remaining funds. Before each bid, I will mentally track: starting budget minus all previous bids equals my true remaining budget.

**On initial lot evaluation:**
When a lot opens in round 1, I will compare my valuation to the estimate and current bid. If my value exceeds the estimate by a meaningful margin (15%+), I will bid to establish presence early rather than pass. Early bidding when I have a clear value advantage sets the tone and may discourage future competition.

**On aggressive bidding when ahead on value:**
When the current high bid is substantially below my valuation (more than 30% below), I will raise to secure the lot rather than bidding minimally. Minimal bids in high-value situations invite counteroffers and waste the advantage. I should bid decisively when I have clear margin.

**On continuation in round 2:**
When round 2 arrives and I'm already committed to a lot, I will bid to win if my valuation still exceeds the current bid by enough to profit after payment. I should not pass just because the price has risen—I should complete the purchase if value remains.

**On lots worth close to or below estimate:**
When a lot is worth 27 to me but carries an estimate of 31, I will be cautious. This signals the lot may not be as strong a value as it appears. I should only bid if the current price is very low relative to my valuation, not relative to the estimate.

**On competitive positioning:**
I will track which bidders are winning lots and at what prices. This helps me identify whether I'm falling behind and need to be more aggressive, or whether I can afford to be selective on remaining lots.

**On final scoring:**
I scored +31 by winning 1 lot at 18 (worth 18 profit) and 1 lot at 18 (worth 9 profit). This suggests selective, disciplined bidding on high-value lots outperforms chasing marginal opportunities.

# Playbook for ref_auction

When I open the bidding on a lot with no prior bids, I bid the minimum raise to establish position while preserving budget.

When the standing bid is significantly below my valuation, I raise to lock in positive expected value, not just the minimum amount.

When deciding whether to continue bidding in a round, I calculate my net gain if I win at the next minimum raise: (my valuation - next bid amount). If this is positive, I bid.

I track my total winnings and spending so far to understand my position relative to other bidders, but I focus my decisions on individual lot value, not on trying to match or beat specific competitors.

When I have remaining rounds after winning a lot, I don't assume my budget is depleted—I calculate what I actually spent and what I have left, then use that for future bidding decisions.

I avoid making bids when my budget calculation is uncertain. If I don't have reliable information about my remaining budget, I should not guess at a large round number like 200000—this signals I've lost track of my actual position.

When a lot is in its final round (round 2/2), I'm more willing to bid to win if the value-to-me significantly exceeds the standing bid, because there will be no further opportunity to acquire similar value.

I bid to win lots where I have positive expected value at the current price, measured by (my valuation - price I'd pay), regardless of whether other bidders have won more lots than me.

# Auction Playbook

When I see my valuation for a lot, I compare it directly to the standing bid. If the standing bid is already at or above my valuation, I pass immediately—don't chase.

When the standing bid is well below my valuation, I bid aggressively in round 1 to establish control. A 25-30% raise above the minimum signals strength and discourages further bidding.

In round 2, if I'm still in contention for a lot worth significantly more to me than the current bid, I raise to secure it. This is my last chance, so I bid confidently rather than with the minimum raise.

When I win a lot, I track my remaining budget carefully. Know exactly what I have left for the remaining lots. Don't lose track of my position mid-auction.

I don't bid just because a lot is worth something to me relative to the estimate. The estimate doesn't matter—only my valuation matters relative to what I'm actually paying. A lot worth 45 to me at a bid of 3 is good; the estimate of 33 is irrelevant.

I watch what other bidders are winning. If one bidder is accumulating most of the lots, that's not my problem—I focus on value for myself, not on "balancing the score."

On the final lot, if it represents good value relative to my remaining budget and my valuation, I bid to win it. Don't leave value on the table just because it's the last round.

I avoid the mistake of chasing lots where the current bid has already exceeded my valuation. Walking away cleanly preserves budget for better opportunities and prevents me from overpaying.
